title: More Clothing Brands Offering Repair Services
paragraphs: In an effort to attract young shoppers and reduce waste, a growing number of clothing brands are offering services to repair customers' clothes.

The American jeans maker Levi's is expanding its "Wear Longer" program across the US, building on the repair and customization services it already offers in hundreds of stores around the world. It also runs a sewing course that teaches high school students how to replace a button, fix a hem and patch holes. Paul Dillinger, the company's head of global design innovation, said it was important to give customers the skills to look after their clothes.

The Japanese brand Uniqlo now offers repairs, traditional sashiko mending, embroidery and restyling in 75 of its roughly 2,500 stores. Meanwhile, the Irish fashion chain Primark has held more than 730 free workshops teaching skills such as replacing zips and buttons, and it has tested in-store repairs at three stores in the UK. Zara, the Spanish fashion brand, allows customers in 17 countries to request basic alterations and repairs through its online platform.

These services are aimed especially at Gen Z, the generation born between 1997 and 2012, many of whom want to save money and reduce their impact on the environment. Retail analyst Neil Saunders of GlobalData said that offering repairs gives a brand a positive image.

The environmental impact of the fashion industry is enormous. According to the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, clothing production roughly doubled between 2000 and 2015, while the number of times each piece of clothing was worn fell by about 36%. Furthermore, less than 1% of the material from discarded clothing is recycled into new clothes.

However, repair services are difficult to run profitably, because mending clothes requires a lot of work and must be offered at a low price. Some experts are also skeptical. Kate Fletcher, a professor of sustainability and fashion at Manchester Metropolitan University, pointed out that repairs happen in addition to growing production, not instead of it.
